instructions: Insomnia is a macOS menu bar app that keeps a MacBook awake for one timed session. A session starts by turning sleep off with pmset -a disablesleep 1 through the macOS administrator password prompt (osascript, AdministratorPrompt.swift); while it runs the app executes sudo -n pmset to turn sleep back on and to switch Low Power Mode, SIGSTOPs other apps' processes when the lid closes, mutes audio, sets the display and keyboard backlight to 0, and writes NSAppSleepDisabled into agent apps' preferences. Every change is journaled in state.json before it is made and is undone from that journal, by the app (reconcile at launch, lid open, session end, Quit) or by scripts/backstop.sh, which a per-user LaunchAgent runs at load and every 60 s with macOS /bin/bash 3.2. The worst bugs leave the Mac in a changed state with nothing able to undo it: a change made before its journal entry is on disk, an entry cleared before the undo was confirmed, a journal the shell can no longer parse, a SIGKILLed sudo, a recovery lock released while a privileged command still runs, or a SIGCONT sent to a process Insomnia did not stop. Weigh those far above style. Read .greptile/rules.md before flagging a design listed there as deliberate.

rules.rule: Any change to power state (pmset disablesleep, through sudo -n or the administrator password prompt, or pmset lowpowermode), to another process (SIGSTOP), to audio output (volume or mute), to display or keyboard brightness, or to another app's NSAppSleepDisabled (AppNap.swift, opt-in) is written to state.json first, through Store.saveState (the journal helper in SessionManager), and that write has returned without error before the change is made. If the write fails the change is not made.

A journal entry in state.json is cleared only after the undo it records has been confirmed: the pmset command exited 0, the SIGCONT was delivered to a verified pid, the audio or brightness write returned without error. A failed, timed-out or unverified undo leaves the entry in place so reconcile or backstop.sh retries it, and a failure to clear an entry after a successful undo is reported to the user and logged, not swallowed with try?.

A change to the keys, types or encoding of state.json (RuntimeState, FrozenProcess) or session.json (Session) also updates journal_shape_problems and the key reads in scripts/backstop.sh and scripts/uninstall.sh, states what the shell does with the new key (undo it, keep it for the app, or ignore it), and adds or changes cases in Tests/InsomniaTests/RecoveryScriptTests.swift. The app's decoder keeps accepting a journal written by an older build or by backstop.sh.

Sleep is disabled (pmset -a disablesleep 1 through the administrator password prompt) only after session.json and the sleepDisabledByUs journal entry are on disk and LaunchdBackstop.arm() has returned without error. A failed arm rolls the start back and never reaches the prompt. Only an explicit Start shows the prompt: reconcile at launch and every other path read pmset -g and never prompt or re-apply disablesleep 1. The LaunchAgent plist at the trusted path only ever holds a plist launchd actually loaded.

The root command behind the password prompt runs as /usr/bin/lockf -k -n -t 10 <pending-start> /bin/sh -c <fixed text>, and runs pmset -a disablesleep 1 only while pending-start holds the nonce of the start that showed the prompt. lockf holds the marker's flock from before that check until pmset exits, and every deleter takes the same lock before it unlinks the file, and unlinks it only while the path still names the file it locked: Store.removePendingStart compares fstat of its locked descriptor with stat of the path and looks again if they differ; backstop.sh and uninstall.sh open the marker on fd 8 (regular files only), lock that descriptor with $LOCKF -s -t N 8, and compare $STAT -f %d:%i <&8 with $STAT -L -f %d:%i of the path before $RM -f. So the marker never goes between the check and the end of pmset. When a stuck prompt is voided, performStart also requires the locked file to be the one savePendingStart wrote (removePendingStart(expecting:)): a file put in its place may have been swapped in after the root command locked the original, and a missing one may have gone without the lock, so neither counts as voided. performStart writes a fresh nonce just before the prompt and deletes the marker on every outcome before it releases the recovery lock (on .stillRunning, before it waits and again after the prompt exits if its command held the lock). Every other holder of the recovery lock deletes it before it reads or clears the journal: exclusive() in the app, backstop.sh right after lockf, uninstall.sh right after lockf and before it runs a possibly older backstop. Nothing deletes it without the recovery lock, because a live start may be waiting on its prompt. sleepDisabledByUs is cleared only after the marker was removed in the same transaction (restoreAll, and the backstop's marker_stuck gate); a marker that cannot be removed keeps the entry, is reported, makes every backstop.sh run exit 1 (a still-valid session and a moved-aside session.json included), refuses new starts and is retried. A cancelled prompt (-128 as osascript's last word) or a launch failure ran nothing as root and is rolled back exactly, with no pmset. SleepGuarding.disableSleep takes a PendingStart, so no path turns sleep off without a marker.

A privileged command (sudo -n pmset, or the osascript behind the administrator password prompt) is never sent SIGKILL, in the app or in the scripts. On timeout it may get SIGTERM, which sudo relays to pmset and waits for, and which takes the password dialog down with osascript. A command still alive after that is left running and reported with its pid, because killing sudo orphans a root pmset that can change power state later, outside any transaction.

The recovery lock (.recovery.lock: flock in RecoveryLock.swift, lockf on fd 9 in the scripts) is not released, and no further undo runs, while a privileged command started under it may still be running and may still change something, or while the app binary that backstop.sh runs for --resume-frozen may still send a signal: that binary keeps the lock on fd 9 and ends itself after the lifetime the shell passes. The one command that no longer can is a password prompt whose pending-start marker the transaction deleted under the marker's own lock: its root command then exits without running pmset, so the start rolls back and releases the lock without waiting for it (SessionManager's stillRunning branch). The lock file is never unlinked or replaced, so every holder locks the same inode. Failing to acquire the lock means doing nothing, never proceeding unlocked.

SIGCONT is sent only to a journaled pid whose recorded identity still matches the live process: start time to the microsecond and boot session in the app, and in the app binary that backstop.sh runs for entries that record startedAtMicros (Insomnia --resume-frozen, with a time limit, run only when the Info.plist of the installed bundle, or with --own-bundle (install.sh, before the swap) of the staged bundle the script is sealed in, declares InsomniaResumeFrozenVersion equal to RESUME_FROZEN_VERSION; a timeout, a missing declaration, or any answer that is not exactly one expected line per entry keeps the entries); start time to the second and boot session in backstop.sh only for entries without startedAtMicros. Provisional entries (identity nil, written before the kernel confirmed the stop) and legacy frozenPids are never signaled and are never cleared by the shell. A pid that cannot be observed stays journaled. One exception: when the write confirming a freeze fails, LidActions.freeze undoes the SIGSTOPs it sent moments earlier through cancelStops, checked against the identity it read before the SIGSTOP and still holds in memory (microseconds and boot session). That SIGCONT goes to a matching pid even if it does not show as stopped yet, because a SIGSTOP can still be pending and generating SIGCONT discards it. That rollback then removes the provisional entries of the pids it resumed, that are gone, or that the freeze never stopped, and keeps those it could not resume.

A child process is started with an absolute executable path and an argument array: Shell.run, Shell.run(timeout:), CancellableCommand.run, or Process with executableURL and arguments. Nothing runs through /bin/sh -c, /bin/bash -c, zsh, osascript with a built command string, or a string that has data interpolated into it. The one AppleScript, AdministratorPrompt.disableSleepScript, is a compile-time literal, and so are the lockf prefix (AdministratorPrompt.markerLock) and the root command it hands to /bin/sh -c (AdministratorPrompt.rootCommand). Their only data, the pending-start marker path and nonce, arrive as osascript arguments and reach the root shell through quoted form of, as lockf's file operand and as $1 and $2; they are compared, never spliced into command text, and nothing read from a file is run. No executable is resolved through PATH; Shell.locate picks from a fixed candidate list of absolute paths.

The scripts run under macOS /bin/bash 3.2 (the LaunchAgent runs backstop.sh with it; install.sh and uninstall.sh run under it) and must parse with /bin/bash -n there. Do not use bash 4 or 5 features: mapfile or readarray, declare -A, ${var,,}, ${var^^}, ${var@Q}, negative array subscripts, wait -n, coproc, or |&. ShellCheck in CI runs on Linux and does not catch these.

Every tool that changes the machine or reads process, power or launchd state is called through the absolute-path variable declared at the top of the script (PMSET, SUDO, PLUTIL, LOCKF, PS, KILL, SYSCTL, PGREP, OSASCRIPT, LAUNCHCTL, CODESIGN, SWIFT, SWIFTC, ICONUTIL, DEFAULTS, INSTALL, RM, RMDIR, MKDIR, CP, MV, MKTEMP, CAT, VISUDO, TEST, STAT), never by bare name through PATH. That includes cleanup in EXIT traps, and commands run through sudo: write `"$SUDO" "$INSTALL"`, not `"$SUDO" install`, because sudo looks a bare name up in the caller's PATH and runs what it finds as root. A new tool gets a new variable in that block, because RecoveryScriptTests and PackagingTests patch exactly those lines in a private copy of the script to substitute fakes. A script's own bounded-call helper may signal the child it started with the shell builtin `kill`; every signal to a process the script did not start goes through `$KILL`.

The file install.sh writes to /etc/sudoers.d/insomnia grants NOPASSWD for exactly these three commands and nothing else: /usr/bin/pmset -a disablesleep 0, /usr/bin/pmset -b lowpowermode 1, /usr/bin/pmset -b lowpowermode 0. No wildcard, no ALL, no bare /usr/bin/pmset, no other command, and it is validated with visudo -cf before it is installed. /usr/bin/pmset -a disablesleep 1 is never passwordless, on any install.sh path including failure and rollback paths: it runs only through the administrator password prompt (AdministratorPrompt.disableSleepScript via /usr/bin/osascript). SleepGuard.swift runs only those three argument lists through sudo, and nothing runs sudo before the prompt: SleepGuarding.checkSleepSettingForStart only reads pmset -g. The root command behind the prompt establishes the passwordless restore before it turns sleep off, without running it: after the nonce and deadline checks, under the marker's lock and before any pmset, root asks the user's sudo (/usr/bin/sudo -n -u "#$4" /usr/bin/env -i LC_ALL=C /usr/bin/sudo, stdin /dev/null) for -V, -k -n -l and -k -n -ll /usr/bin/pmset -a disablesleep 0, and runs /usr/bin/pmset -a disablesleep 1 only if sudo is 1.9.15 to 1.9.x with only the sudoers plugins, the listing shows no Runas or command-specific Defaults, and the -ll answer is exactly the /etc/sudoers.d/insomnia entry (RunAsUsers: root, Options: !authenticate, the restore as its only command, Matched: the restore), with the deadline checked again after the queries and right before the write. Otherwise it exits 5 with no pmset run and the start rolls back with nothing to undo (AdministratorPromptError.restoreNeedsPassword), so sleep is never turned off while the passwordless restore is missing. Nothing treats a generic sudo -l, sudo -v, a bare exit status or a NOPASSWD grep as proof, because a listing passes for commands that still need a password. install.sh runs no pmset; after writing the rule it checks a sudo -k -n -l listing of the three commands. install.sh writes the file only under the recovery lock, after the running app has quit, so every stop before the write leaves the previous rule beside the previous app. README.md, SECURITY.md and docs/spec.md list the same three and the prompt.

A behavior change comes with a regression test in Tests/InsomniaTests that exercises the changed path and asserts the observable outcome (journal contents, the fake's recorded calls and their order, the script's exit code and the journal it leaves), not only that a mock method was called. App code is tested through the injected system dependencies and the fakes in TestSupport.swift with a temporary journal (TempHome, INSOMNIA_HOME); scripts are tested through a patched private copy with fake tools, as RecoveryScriptTests and PackagingTests do.

A test never runs pmset with arguments that change a setting, never signals a process it did not start itself, never reads, adds or deletes login Keychain items, never writes another app's preferences (CFPreferences or defaults), never runs install.sh, uninstall.sh, backstop.sh or simulate-lid.sh unpatched against the real home, and never touches ~/Library/Application Support/Insomnia, ~/Library/LaunchAgents or /etc. tmux cases use a private server socket, not the contributor's panes.

Nothing user-identifying reaches the unified log (os.Logger) as public: no SSID or hotspot name, tmux target or pane id, process name, bundle id, app name, path under the home directory, or pane content. Such values keep the default private privacy; only fixed phrases, counts, numbers and error kinds may be marked privacy: .public. The plain-text insomnia.log file is a separate local file and may hold them (SECURITY.md).

A row in the 'Hardware validation still required' table changes from 'Not run' only together with the tested commit, hardware, macOS version, date and observed result written into the same file. New behavior that needs a check on real hardware adds a 'Not run' row. Passing tests, a source review or a green CI run are never recorded as hardware evidence.

Docs, comments and user-facing strings use no em dashes or en dashes (end the sentence or use a comma), sentence-case headings, plain words (not crucial, robust, seamless, leverage, utilize, or ensure as filler), active voice, the mechanism before the feeling, and actual numbers where they exist. UI copy is short and says what happens.
